overview.text: Damping is the gradual decrease in an oscillator’s motion when forces such as friction or drag remove mechanical energy. It explains why real swings, spring systems, and plucked guitar strings do not keep moving forever without added energy. In lightly damped motion, the oscillator continues back and forth while its amplitude shrinks; the lost energy is often converted to heat. In a common mathematical model, drag is proportional to speed and the amplitude fades exponentially, though real damping forces do not always follow that simple rule. Stronger damping can stop the back-and-forth motion entirely, and controlled damping is useful in devices such as car shock absorbers.

key_facts.text: Damping forces oppose motion and reduce an oscillator’s mechanical energy; some of that energy is commonly transferred as heat.
With light damping, the amplitude decreases while the period and frequency remain nearly the same as in undamped motion.
For a common model where drag is proportional to speed, amplitude decays exponentially; actual damping forces do not always follow this model.
Underdamped systems keep oscillating as they settle; with sufficiently strong damping, a system moves toward equilibrium without oscillating.
Car shock absorbers use damping to reduce unwanted motion and help a vehicle’s suspension settle.
